$comment: England & Wales, Medical Law - informed consent, capacity as the gateway (MCA 2005 s.1) and material-risk disclosure (Montgomery). Fresh research this session. Montgomery is a Scottish appeal but its ratio on informed consent has been treated as stating the common law of England & Wales too, reconciling the English authorities Bolam and Sidaway - noted honestly rather than treated as a purely domestic E&W case. Both nodes are post-2005/2015 and fetched directly, no BAILII/pre-2009 access issue to route around.

authorities.name: Mental Capacity Act 2005, s.1 - the principles
authorities.date_note: Date s.1 came fully into force. The text verified this session is the current in-force version.
authorities.proposition: Before any question of risk disclosure under Montgomery can matter, a patient must have legal capacity to decide. S.1 sets five governing principles: capacity is presumed; a person is not treated as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed; an unwise decision is not itself evidence of incapacity; anything done for an incapacitated person must be in their best interests; and any intervention must be the least restrictive option achieving its purpose. This is the statutory gateway determining whether Montgomery's disclosure duty is being discharged to a person capable of exercising genuine autonomous choice.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session on two independent passes (summary and as-enacted text), word-for-word consistent on subsections (2) and (4).

authorities.name: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Kerr and Lord Reed (joint leading judgment)
authorities.proposition: Abandoned the Bolam (professional-practice) standard for a doctor's duty to warn a patient of risks. A doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risk in a proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives. Materiality is tested by whether a reasonable person in the patient's position would likely attach significance to the risk, or the doctor knows or should know this particular patient would - a patient-centred, not doctor-centred, test. The duty involves genuine dialogue, not discharged merely by providing technical information or a signed consent form.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly from Find Case Law this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches word-for-word consistent on paragraph 87's materiality test. Cross-checked against 4 independent academic secondary sources (Oxford Academic Medical Law Review, two PMC articles, Law Society of Scotland Journal) which independently reproduce the identical para 87 wording.

edges.verified_via: Montgomery's disclosure duty presupposes a capacitous patient - the MCA 2005 s.1 capacity threshold gates whether Montgomery's material-risk test even applies, rather than the best-interests regime for incapacitated patients.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes covering capacity as a gateway and material-risk disclosure once capacity exists. Does not cover the best-interests test for incapacitated patients in detail, clinical negligence causation (Bolitho), end-of-life decision-making, or any other Medical Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
